utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Mikulicic, is the Markac Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I take it that it will be Zoran Cvrk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Cvrk is our next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Cvrk. Before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration of which the text will now be handed out to you by the usher. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cvrk. Please be seated. Mr. Cvrk, you will first be examined by Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic is counsel for Mr. Markac. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Cvrk.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Good morning, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Cvrk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would ask the Registry for 3D00886. Mr. Cvrk, you will see a document on the screen shortly and that is your statement which you gave to the Defence of General Markac. You remember that you gave the statement to the Defence of General Markac, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That was on 13th of May this year, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could we please see the last page of this statement. You also remember, Mr. Cvrk, that you signed that statement as the one you gave?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature, the one you see on the right-hand side of the screen?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvrk, when you gave the statement, did you say everything to the best of your knowledge and recollection about the facts and the truth?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: To my best knowledge and recollection, in connection with the events and the military and police Operation Storm, I expressed everything truthfully, all the facts and the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you the same questions today, and if we discussed the same topics, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I propose to tender this statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1833.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1833 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvrk, please be so kind so as to describe briefly your professional development. What is your education, where did you work, and what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: I was born in Osijek in 1965. That was where I completed primary school. And then I enrolled the general military high school Ivo Lola Ribar in Zagreb, which I completed in 1984. After that I enrolled at the Land Forces Military Academy in Belgrade. And in 1988, I completed this as anti-aircraft sublieutenant in Zadar and I worked in the 155th Rocket Regiment of anti-aircraft defence which was based in Zagreb, and the unit I was in was in Stubicka Slatina. At the beginning of the war, I held the rank of lieutenant and then I was transferred to the police. In the police I started working in the special unit of the Zagreb police administration and I was a specialist training instructor, that was my post. And in 1993, by a decision of the interior ministry, I was appointed commander of the same unit. Between 1993 and the year 2000, I was the commander of the special unit of the Zagreb police administration, known as Alpha, and in the meantime, between late 1996 and the summer of 1998, I was special police unit commander in the police forces attached to the UN administration for the Croatian Danube Valley area. In the year 2002, I became director of the Security Staff of the Office of National Security, and I dealt with counter-intelligence protection of protected persons in the Republic of Croatia until the year 2002, when I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I could please see the document 3D00321.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvrk, you told us that you joined the special police unit of the Zagreb police administration where you were an instructor and that then in 1993 you were appointed commander of this unit. Mr. Cvrk, in front of you, you will see a document of the 27th of May, 1993, according to which the assistant chief of the Zagreb police administration proposes to the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Croatia that you be appointed to the post of the commander of the special police unit within this police administration. Mr. Cvrk, please, tell me was this the usual way to propose persons for specific posts within the police administration via the assistant chief or chief?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Yes, the appointment of the commander of the special police unit, as my superior was the chief of the police administration in the Zagreb police administration, it was usual that that police administration do that. And in this case, you can see that this document was signed by the assistant chief for personnel, Mr. Misetic, proposed to the minister of the interior who would be appointed to which post. So that was the usual way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And as for the administrative duty of appointing someone or relieving someone of their post, the sector of special police and its chief or the deputy or assistant chief of police administration, did they have any influence or administrative role in appointment to the post that you were assigned to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: In the administrative sense certainly not, but I believe that professionally they may have been consulted by the persons who appointed me, that is to say, the interior minister, whether I fulfilled the general criteria in terms of ability and some other criteria so that I could be appointed the commander of the police special unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your position as the commander of the special police unit attached to the Zagreb police administration, is in the terms of hierarchy, subordinated to whom?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: In terms of hierarchy, my position as the commander of the special police unit of the Zagreb police administration was subordinated to the chief of the Zagreb police administration. I was directly subordinated to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could now please see the document D1086 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: From the previous document we could see that the proposal for your appointment was sent to the minister of the interior and now we shall see the decision of the minister of the interior according to which Zoran Cvrk is appointed as of the 15th of June, 1993, to the post of commander of the special unit of the Zagreb police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please scroll down the Croatian version so that we could see the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Cvrk, in the lower right-hand corner you will see that the minister of the interior, Mr. Jarnjak, signed this document. And in the left-hand corner you will see that it was delivered to yourself, to the police administration in Zagreb, and to the archives. So the minister of the interior directly appointed you, and there is no doubt about that. Please, tell us whether this appointment as the commander of the special police unit within the Zagreb police administration was also submitted to the special police sector, because here we cannot see it from the document, that is to say, we see that it was not submitted, was this usual or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: This was the usual personnel policy of the Ministry of the Interior and certainly in one way or another the special police sector was informed about this. However, the whole thing developed just as we can see from the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Later on we will talk a bit about the relations within the special police sector. However, before that, let me ask you this, and the easiest way will be to establish that through documents I will show you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please see D1084, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvrk, now you will see an order from 1991 which was issued by the then interior minister, Mr. Ivan Vekic. The order is dated from late 1991, from the month of November. And in the order, in item 1, it is stated that special police units should be set up in each police administration for special reasons of security. Further on, under number 7, it is mentioned that special units are to be engaged solely pursuant to decisions issued by the chief of a police administration and deputy minister of the interior or the person thus authorised by him. Mr. Cvrk, according to your knowledge, recollection and experience, was this sort of practice which was introduced by the order from 1991, was implemented continually during your work in the special police?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: This order confirms the manner of engagement of the special police unit of the interior ministry within police administrations. Most of the engagement since 1991 and 1992 were in the area of the police administrations, and in the sense of establishment and command, everything that was connected with the special police in these years was mostly connected with the local police administrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we could now please have a look at the second page of this document, we will see under item 8 in the English version, it's the last paragraph on the page that question certainly see. It says here, Mr. Cvrk, that the chief of a police administration, before engaging a special unit in the area of his administration, must obtain clearance from deputy minister or the person authorised by the deputy minister. And then under item 9, it says that the special unit cannot be engaged in the area of the another police administration without a decision issued by the deputy minister. Was that the usual way to engage a special police unit, Mr. Cvrk?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Even though at the time I was the instructor of special training, that is to say, I was second in the chain of command, I can say with certainty that that was the usual way that any special police unit within any police administration was used and that it was very logical that this kind of unit could not be engaged without the knowledge of the commanding leadership. And that is to say, the deputy minister of the interior ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could now please see the document D1077.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvrk, what I will show you now is the Law on Internal Affairs which was published in mid-1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if we could please Article 24 of this law which is on page 3 -- no, page 4 of the Croatian version of the text, Article 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That is the article, Mr. Cvrk, which Mr. Jarnjak referred in the order on your appointment as the legal basis, and this article actually says that because of special reasons of security the maintenance or establishment of law and order in the event of an emergency caused by a natural disaster or an epidemic, the enactment establishing a special unit shall designate which employees of the ministry shall make up the special unit. At the time, that is to say, in 1991, in this law, the term "special police" is not expressly mentioned but, rather, "special units." However, in the amendment to this law which came into force in 1994, and for reference this is P1148, this Article was changed and special police was expressly mentioned and which is established to fight all forms of sabotage and terrorist activities in order to prevent the kidnapping of persons or vehicles, in order to liberate hostages and do other duties from the area of work of the ministry under special conditions. Does this correspond to the practice which you performed as the commander of special police units?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Yes, that is absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that you were first an instructor, a specialist training instructor. Can you please tell us, in a few sentences, what kind of post was that, and what duties did you perform as a specialist training instructor?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Well, you see, at the beginning of the homeland war and when the special police units were formed, not even the internal structure of special police was very solid in the sense of chain of command and the precision of the duties for each post that we had. In brief, the specialist training instructor could be in the special police unit of the Zagreb police administration. He could be a person who had to work with the men up to a reinforced platoon, or he could be a person who, by his specialisation and specific military and police knowledge, was in charge of training. I was in charge both of training and I was in charge of the men. So I had a clear structure of the people who were subordinated to me and that I was a commander to. The documents that you showed were a realist precondition for the creation of the special police sector which, as an organisational structure, was only later set up as of 1993 onwards and only then were the duties and the tasks clearly stated, as well as the ranks, the chain of command, and the internal structure of every special police unit in any police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now we will touch on the subject of the internal structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if we could please see the document D527 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You will see, Mr. Cvrk, now a decree on the internal structure and the manner of work of the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Croatia from the month of February 1995, where, in Article 2 of the decree, it says that in order to conduct affairs pursuant to the Law on Internal Affairs, the following offices shall be established in the ministry, and then we can see the office of the cabinet, the minister's office and the sector. When you mentioned sector a while ago, please tell us what kind of an organisational unit was the special police sector, and according to your best knowledge and recollection, why was such a form selected?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: The decree governing the internal structure and work of the Ministry of Interior did not set out the provisions concerning the special police sector only. There were -- there was the police sector, the crime police sector, the administrative affairs sector, the personnel and legal sectors. There were several such sectors. One of the ways in which the Ministry of Interior was structured was to include the special police sector, which, according to the new structure, was given the task of detailing all the tasks that would fall within the remit of the special police structure, or force, as one of the forces coming under the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now turn to Article 27 of the decree, which is at page 15 of the English version in e-court. Article 27 relates to the special police sector. The Croatian version is on 3D001513. That's the page number. Article 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We're waiting for the English version before I start reading it, Mr. Cvrk. The Article reads as follows: The special police sector establishes, manages, and directs the work of special police units, proposes the most efficient methods and means, adopts the plan and means of specialist training, and checks the level of combat readiness and enforcement of legal provisions achieved. Mr. Cvrk, this particular provision describes the duties of the special police units. How did you apply them in practice, and to you, as a commander of a special police unit within the Zagreb police administration, how did this hierarchy appear?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: These guidelines in accordance with the structure of the Ministry of Interior, were in fact duties of the special police sector and all the special police units. Under the law, the special police units were supposed to carry out these duties, train their men, honour the hierarchy, and take care of all the employees or, rather, members of the special police sector. They were supposed to be prepared for the duties of enforcing law and order. Whenever it was disrupted it was supposed to provide assistance to the general duty police and crime police. And it was supposed to, of course, be specialised in terrorist combat, combat in urban areas, knowledge of tactics and the relevant legal provisions, report to the special police sector on all its duties, and cover all the activities -- monitor all the activities that its units are engaged in. It was also duty-bound to keep a record of all the activities and all the documents governing its structure and activity throughout its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could it be said that this was in fact a specialist hierarchy, a specialist line of command, as it were?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Yes, quite clearly it was a specialist line -- chain of command or hierarchy within the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you spoke of the internal structure of the Ministry of the Interior, you referred several sectors, including the police sector, the crime police sector, the special police sector, et cetera. From comparison's sake, let's look at the way in which this same decree resolves the duties of the crime police sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's turn to Article 17, which is at page 10 of the version in e-court. This is where the crime police sector is defined -- or let us just wait for the text to appear. Page 10 of e-court and the Croatian version is 3D001510. That's the page number of the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is how the decree governs the work of the crime police sector. It is supposed to monitor and examine the trend in criminality in general, cooperate with other ministries, and crime investigation services, provide professional and technical assistance, control the work of police administrations, particular in terms of crime prevention, et cetera. Mr. Cvrk, the fact that the sector was structured in this way, within the Ministry of Interior, and I'm referring to the crime police sector, if we compare it to the way the special police sector was structured, do you notice any similarities or, in other words, what would your comments on this score be?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: There are definitely similarities, primarily within the -- in terms of the specialist organisation. The lower level structure is a department. Although, of course, the duties there with which the criminal police is quite different from that of the special police. We can see that the structure envisages that below the level of the sector there would be various departments charged with different matters, and this is shared by both sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can we say, then, that the way in which the sectors were organised within the Ministry of Interior was envisaged in a such way that they should cover each their own specialist field of activity?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at D1083, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cvrk --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited to make a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will do my best, Your Honour. I'm sorry to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see here the rules governing the internal order of the Ministry of the Interior, dating from the 17th of November, 1995. The rules detail the internal organisation and work posts within the ministry. Let us look at the way in which the commander of the special police unit was defined as a post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which is at page 5 of the Croatian version and page 6 of the English version. The Croatian version starts at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Commander of the special police unit shall, directly manage and be held responsible for the work of the special police unit, plan, organise, coordinate, and direct all actions involving the participation of the special police unit. Further down, it is stated that it will propose to the chief of the police administration the way in which the personnel is to be recruited, and will recruit the personnel as per the criteria defined. On completed action, he is duty-bound to report in writing to the chief of the police administration and to the chief of the special police sector on the action carried out. Further down, it is stated that he is responsible for the discipline, detection of any negative events, incidents within the unit, and suggest to his superior on measures to be taken. Finally, it said that he is duty-bound to monitor the cutting-edge achievements of similar police units in other countries and make suggestions to his superior accordingly. Mr. Cvrk, can you tell us, as the commander of a special police unit, whether these were indeed the tasks that your unit was addressing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Yes. This fully tallies with the description of the duties that I discharged as commander of the special police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvrk, now that we have defined the relations within the Ministry of Interior, or specifically within the police administration, can you tell us whether the same relations applied to the engagement of special police units in peacetime circumstances, as well as in circumstances of combat, such as the ones that existed in the police and military Operation Storm, or was there a special set-up envisaged for such circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Clearly, the special police units had clearly defined tasks within their respective police administrations in relation to the tasks that they were supposed to discharge outside of the area of responsibility of the police administration. There was a clear hierarchy which started from the chief of the police administration or basically the Deputy Chief of the police administration. He was the first operative officer who was there on behalf of his specialist field, either the crime police or the special police unit, and he was supposed to be responsible for the regular duties discharged by the special police as well as those out of the ordinary activities. When we're talking about the regular activities, that is to say, the enforcement of public law and order and other regular police duties, and this concerned the duties within one's own area of responsibility of one's own police administration, such as police raids, police activities in combat against terrorism or arrest of perpetrators of the most serious crimes, through to the most difficult situations for the police, such as hostage situations, for instance. In other words, all these documents that we've just looked at clearly defined the chain of command. Now, when it came to different situations where special police unit members had to be put together and dispatched outside of the area of responsibility of their own police administration, for instance, in my -- in the case of my own unit, when we were supposed to provide assistance to the crime police of our administration or of the Ministry of Interior in general, in such cases we were supposed to be given a clear authorisation in the Ministry of Interior in order to be able to leave our AOR and engage in such high-risk scenarios, such as football matches where unrest was expected. We, as the unit of the police -- of the Zagreb police administration, we were trained to deal with such situations. Or, in the case of Operations Flash and Storm, we were given clear instructions and authorisations as to the reasons for our leaving our AOR and the authorisation to leave our AOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the engagement of special police units together with other forces in general, we will deal with this matter later on. Let us now discuss special police as one of the forces within the Ministry of Interior which had to have specialist knowledge and training. As for the training which related to special police force, in what way were members of the special police force trained in different specialist skills and knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Well, as we saw before, the specialist chain of command was clearly defined, which tasked every unit commander with the duty to carry out specialist training within his own respective chain of command. Every unit kept a diary of specialist training which included specialist fields of training and there was specific instructors charged with given fields. They were in charge of training. The training plan was monitored throughout the year for the level of its achievement in each and every special police units. The purpose of the whole exercise was to see to what extent the training plan had been carried out. There was an inspection task force within the special police structure which was charged with specifically monitoring the course of training.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up document 3D00729.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The issue of training and schooling of special police units is dealt with here. This is a document dated from 1992, which the then chief of the special police department, Mr. Mladen Markac, sent to the assistant minister, Mr. Josko Moric. The subject is the request for special police unit members to be authorised to attend courses at the faculty of criminal justice sciences. In this particular letter, the chief of the special police department seeks authorisation from the assistant minister to allow his men to be additionally schooled at a university. Was this something that was not only typical for 1992 but was present in the subsequent years throughout your term of office there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: This is one of the documents whereby the then special police department, which was later to become the special police sector, addresses the right addressee up the chain of command, and this was Mr. Josko Moric, assistant minister at the time, to -- to allow special police unit members to attend regular courses at the police academy. They had courses for criminology, and this was the particular course where those police officers who were in good health and had completed the secondary school, could attend courses, full time or part time, in order to gain specialist knowledge, and they would then acquire the title of graduate criminologist or merely a criminologist for undergraduate

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1834.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1834 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. If we could please see the document 3D00731 on the screen now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now we will see another document dealing with the same subject, from January 1995, also submitted to the minister of the interior, Mr. Ivan Jarnjak, asking for approval for professional training of the leader of the special units of the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Croatia, where it is mentioned that the sector of the special police - previously it was the department, now it's a sector - planned to establish a special training course for approximately 60 executives of the MUP's special police. What is your recollection of the organisation of courses, which included improvement of special police unit members, how frequent were these courses, was there a number of those, or was this a unique case? Can you tell us something more about that, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: This was just one of the documents which shows a continuous will, wish, intention, to implement professional improvement through all organisational structures of special police. As early as 1992, the first specific specialist courses for leaders within special police were organised so that they would gain the necessary knowledge and military expertise, for the simple reason that all of our members were mostly policemen. These were men who had been prepared to carry out police duties. They were younger men, in terms of age. They had some military knowledge, and they were now actively involved in defending their homeland. By analysing the special police sector, it was very easy to notice the need to educate the members, and especially the leadership, so that they would have all the skills necessary to lead the men, and this is specifically one of the courses for which approval was requested. And we should say that the courses were at first organised at police academy, some of them in specific special police bases, depending on whether these bases were properly equipped for that or not. And in late 1994, if I'm not mistaken, a special training centre was set up near [indiscernible] on Losinj and that what was where all the courses were organised from then onwards, such as courses focussed on law, also on mountaineering or scuba-diving, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber wonders whether all of the information you are presenting at this moment is of such relevance and whether it's contested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't gain the impression that the training at the various levels of responsibility was something the Prosecution relied upon as being insufficient. And therefore, we now know that the training took place on Losinj. What are we supposed to do with this information, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to demonstrate that the special police, since its establishment, was continuously trained and had undergone specialist training and that specialisation and professionalism were insisted on. If this is not contested in any way, I think that my learned friend agrees about this, then I just wish to refer you to the document D528, in which the number and kind of courses that were organised for members of special police are specified. However, if we could now please see from document D528, page 28 in English version, and we will change the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvrk --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, let's verify. Ms. Mahindaratne, the document just mentioned is also not contested --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as far as content is concerned. Then please move on, Mr. Mikulicic. I thought in the beginning that, and I briefly consulted with my colleagues, that perhaps you need a kind of an introduction, even if it's to some extent even what we find already in the written statement. But it took forms now, over the last 45 minutes, such a way that the Chamber really thinks that it's -- that we better focus on what is contested and what are the real issues in this case. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] If we could please see page 30 in the Croatian version, and page 28 in the English version in the document D528.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As we will see, Mr. Cvrk, this is a report relating to the disciplinary measures taken against the members of the special police, so we will talk about discipline within the special police unit that you were heading. What was your function as the commander of a special police unit, in terms of discipline, what were your obligations, what was your authority? And if any of the members of the special police unit committed any infringement of discipline, how did you react to that and how did you participate in this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: All members of the Ministry of the Interior were held responsible according to a disciplinary set of rules which clearly stated which were the minor and which were the major infringements of discipline. The minister of the interior transferred some of the authority that he had to the heads of police administrations, and the chief of the Zagreb police administration transferred the authority to leaders of some units, whether these were police stations or special police units or some other structural forms such as departments or sectors. The procedure was the following: When the infringements were minor, then one could caution those members or a fine could be imposed on them; or if these were major infringements, then the procedure is something that I would need to initiate, and I would send files to a disciplinary court which was part of the police administration as the first-instance body, and then it was forwarded if someone appealed within 15 days to the second-instance body which was at the seat of the Ministry of the Interior. That was the usual procedure for all members of the unit that I commanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was the procedure of initiating disciplinary responsibility specific in any way for the special police, or was it implemented at the level of the ministry for all organisational structures equally?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: No. It was the single disciplinary procedure which was always applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could turn a page in the document that we see on the screen --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go one page forward in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We'll see a table with statistical data of disciplinary procedures against members of the special police in 1995. Mr. Cvrk, you said that the reports were drafted annually. Is this report about disciplinary measures also something that was drafted annually, or are we talking about a different time-period?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Report about the activities of the unit training and also disciplinary proceedings were monthly, as far as I remember. This is a part of the annual report which we also had to submit to the special police sector. And you can see here what was the manning level of the units, what were the minor and major disciplinary infringements, and also the number of the disciplinary proceedings that were conducted, in terms of the reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The data relating to your unit, we can see that at the bottom of the page, that's the data about the special police unit of the Zagreb police administration, and from the data it follows that your unit, in 1995, was manned with 237 policemen, that there was proceedings relating to 11 minor infringements and 18 major ones which was a total of 12.23 per cent. By comparison with special police units from other police administration, the result within your police administration points to what sort of conclusion? What conclusion can you draw about the frequency of discipline infringements and how serious were they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: One should say that the number of police members, 237, was something relating to the number of 250 of active servicemen we should normally have, and we had 288 members of reserve forces rather than 250. The number of infringements did not depend on the number of members, it depended on the number of individuals who committed any infringements, whether they were members of the active force or the reserve forces. And the data just shows that the command structure of the unit and myself implemented the disciplinary rules of the Croatian MUP and that we tried to maintain discipline at the highest possible level within the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please go back for a second to the document which we already saw and that was the Law on Internal Affairs, and that is D1077. If we could please see Article 80 which deals with the disciplinary responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvrk, the basic Law on Internal Affairs provides disciplinary responsibility in chapter 5. These are Articles 80 to 92, and as you said, it says there that there can be minor and major infringements of work discipline, that the disciplinary courts shall be set up within the police administrations as the first instances, and then a second instance within the ministry. And in Article 84, it is provided that the first-instance disciplinary court would comprise the president and two members of the Chamber, and the second instance of the president and four members. Article 87 provides that disciplinary measures such as public caution or fine or termination of duty can be applied. What kind of disciplinary measure could you take as a commander of a unit, Mr. Cvrk?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Personally, I could take the disciplinary measures relating to minor infringements of discipline and in my authority was to take the measure of public caution or a fine, which were used for minor infringements of discipline. For major infringements, as well as for incidents in which certain members or reserve members were suspected of participating in certain crimes, my duty was to initiate criminal proceedings with all the evidence that such a crime was committed before the disciplinary court of the Zagreb police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In Article 90 of this law, a decision on suspension of duty is mentioned. What were the cases when a policeman could be suspended from duty?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: The minister of the interior or a person that he would authorise, and that was most often the chief of a police administration, in case when major infringements of discipline were committed, or in particular, if crimes were committed, in according the Criminal Code of the Republic of Croatia could suspend someone from duty by a decision which could come into force immediately or in eight days, in which case personal weapons and badge or identity card of a member of the MUP were taken away from this person, if there was evidence that such a crime had been committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us try to give an example from practice. If would you be informed, for example, by the crime police or the investigating judge, that there was suspicion that one of the members of your special unit had committed a crime, what was the procedure that, in such a situation, you would apply?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: In such a situation the procedure was very simple. The procedure would be initiated before the first-instance disciplinary court within the police administration of Zagreb, and the policeman would be suspended from duty. His rights would be that he would be receiving 50 per cent of his salary, so the salary would be docked. He had right to legal assistance during the proceedings. He would be suspended from duty. And if he was suspected of having committed certain crimes, or had committed major infringement of discipline which had grave consequences on the operation of any section of the MUP, then he would be suspended. And the disciplinary court would, independently, conduct the proceedings without any influences from outside, whether these were professional or otherwise. So disciplinary courts were wholly independent from the hierarchy and chain of command of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would such a procedure be conducted in a situation in which criminal proceedings were initiated before a relevant court against one of your members?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: That's right. That was the procedure in such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvrk, let us move on to another topic briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, if would you not mind, I would like to go back to the statistics and conclusions you asked the witness to draw from them. That was the last page of the report, page 29 out of ... Could we have that on our screen again. It was the previous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D528. Page 30 in Croatian and 28 in the English version. The next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's -- in English, it's page 29 out of -- yes, perhaps if you -- Yes. You drew the conclusion that -- that discipline was maintained at the highest possible level. That was your conclusion, in Zagreb. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My conclusion was that all of the commanders in their respective units were duty-bound to implement disciplinary rules and procedures. We were also supposed to monitor the level of discipline and maintain it at the highest possible level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do agree with you. You said, We tried to maintain them at the highest possible level. How could you conclude this from these numbers? Could you give me the reasoning behind how these numbers can show what you tried to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the counsel's question and the data in the table, it is clear that this was not a situation where discipline was not being monitored and followed. This is a living organism, and every individual could have been instituted proceedings against, in disciplinary terms, if an offence had been committed. This was used to raise the awareness of all that discipline is a priority in the work of any commander. This is what this table shows. The total number of measures as well as the indication that there were both minor and major infringements only goes to prove that we were no exemption from the rules that were otherwise applied across the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now let me try to give you three or four different interpretation of these numbers, and then, again, we are talking about how you can draw conclusions. One of the things you could conclude that if, in certain units, the percentage of people that had to be -- that had disciplinary action taken against, if that moves up to 40 per cent and above, the disciplinary system was not functioning at all, or very badly functioning. I'm just -- I'm not saying it is the right conclusion but just to put to you another way of looking at these numbers. Would you say that is logically not conclusive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Each piece of statistical information, including this one, can be interpreted in different ways. The example here is something that was generated by the sector of the special police. I was merely trying to interpret it in the way that it was visible and it was clear that there was much attention paid to discipline. I said that disciplinary measures were undertaken depending on the nature and number of minor and major infringements, independently of the size of the units and its staffing strength. The statistics in and of itself may or may not mean much. However, it exists, and this was a measure of continuously monitoring discipline. This was only one of the ways of reporting for the special police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm talking about drawing conclusions on the basis of number, nothing else. Not to -- I have no -- if you would say, One of the conclusions you could draw from these numbers, that there was an alarming situation in Zagreb because the percentage of severe cases was far higher than the percentage of light cases, which is an alarming situation, would you, from a point of view of logic, could you say that that is not a logical conclusion? Apart from whether it is right or not. But is there anything wrong with the logic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely the purpose of disciplinary monitoring. In relation to minor and major infringements of discipline, it needs to be used to indicate whether discipline in this or that particular unit is of a satisfactory level. I can tell that you certain annual reports, say for 1994, were clear indications of the situation in certain units which, in turn, resulted in staffing changes. That would be one of the clearest indications when looking at such statistics. Professionally speaking, it could indicate the level of satisfaction or dissatisfaction concerning the status of each and every unit of the special police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You further mentioned that the reserves operatives were not 250 but 288; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, sir. Our staffing strength was supposed to have been 250 per establishment; whereas, we actually had 287 staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what -- in what way does that affect the -- because the number, which was 287, apparently not 288, but 287 were actually serving in the reserve forces. Now, if you have more men than the 250 you were supposed to have, what does that say about up-keeping standards of discipline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The staffing strength which exceeded the numbers per establishment was because each unit, including its reserve forces, is a living organism. The figure of 287 at that moment included a number of the policemen who, at that period of time, were already on their way out of the unit, returning to their other duties or studies. Whereas, some of them were on sick-leave as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You raised this matter in the context of the conclusions you have drawn from these numbers. My question to you is: In which way does the fact that you have 287 persons in the reserve force, in what way does that affect the data we find here and, therefore, in what way does it affect any conclusions to be drawn from this table?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The increased number of staff requires great care and responsibility. This number of staff and proceedings is a piece of statistics. As I told you already, each one of us was tasked with implementing the disciplinary rules of the MUP, irrespective of the size of the unit. Each of the commanders implemented the rules of procedure in relation to the minor and major violations of discipline. The size of a particular unit does not have a direct relation to the number of proceedings whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My last question is the following: Isn't it true that to draw any conclusions you would have to know how many violations there had been? I mean, just to give you an example, if a unit reports 10 per cent violations and another unit reports 40 per cent violations, well, if you do not know how many violations there had been, could you draw any conclusions from the reported numbers? Let's just assume, for example, that the 40 per cent reporting reflects a situation in which 40 per cent of the members did act in violation of disciplinary rules; whereas, where 10 per cent was reported, also 40 per cent actually had committed acts in violation of discipline, would you agree with me that, if you don't know what the real numbers are, that it is very difficult to draw any conclusions as to the -- whether or not the discipline was maintained at the highest level or that such efforts were made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we are discussing figures, and if 60 staff committed 26 violations throughout that year, which would result in 40 per cent of the staff having committed any type of infringement, that would be an alarming piece of information. That's what this table is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The table is about what was reported, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is. There is no other data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I'm not saying that the conclusion from this witness may not have been perfect, but there is no way, on the basis of the numbers, to establish that. I just wanted to draw your attention also to the level in which these interpretations of statistics assists the Chamber without having a lot of other information in relation to that same material as well. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] I would kindly ask for 3D00236.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvrk, you mentioned as one of the measures in a disciplinary procedure was fines, imposing fines. I am showing you a document stipulating the criteria for monetary fine, vis-a-vis special police members. Its articles precisely define the percentage of a monthly salary that can be deducted after having committed a certain type of disciplinary violation. Mr. Cvrk, did you, in the course of your work, apply these criteria?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Yes. This was a general instruction so that the commanders could apply a uniform approach in imposing fines for minor violations of discipline, that they could take on as part of their overall duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask that this document be admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1835.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we only have a couple of minutes left before the break, Mr. Cvrk, perhaps we can say something briefly about the appearance of special police members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For that purpose, I would kindly ask for P329, page 2 of the document. It is the Official Gazette of the Republic of Croatia, the edition with the rules about uniforms, insignia and other designations of the special forces units of the MUP. We clearly see what the number -- what the colour of the uniform of special police forces was supposed to be in Articles 6 and onwards, as well as the colour of individual items of clothing. One notices that green prevails in that uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvrk, did members of the special police forces wear the same uniforms as per these rules?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Yes. Based on these rules, all active and reserve staff of the special police wore the same uniforms, and we had a uniform insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were there any rank designations on the special police forces uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Yes. We had uniform rank designations for each and every special police unit, its sectors and departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I may not have been sufficiently clear in my question. If we compare the uniforms worn by the special police with those worn by members of the Croatian Army, as you have just said, you told us that the special police uniforms had designations of individual work posts. But in terms of rank as usually seen in the army, could that be easily seen on police uniforms of that kind?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: No. Any rank designations within the special police was separately designated depending on the job title, such as group leader, instructor or specialty training, assistant deputy, deputy of the special police forces. Each work post had its own designation and insignia in addition to the insignia of the -- our individual special units and the patches of the Ministry of the Interior as well as the patch of the coat of arms of our unit on the right-hand shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may suggest this will be a time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is time for a break. We will have a break until five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the record, the first document that I called up was 3D00321, and this is, in fact, already an exhibit, D1085. I just wanted to clarify this for the record. Similarly, the document I showed to the witness, 3D00731, which deals with professional training of special police units, I would like to tender that document into evidence. 3D00731, that's at transcript page 18, line 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now 3D00321, was assigned a number again or I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not -- so therefore it's just for the record, for our information --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just for the record file, yes, Your Honour. This is D1084.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, my mistake. This is D1085.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what you said a second ago. So that's now on the record. Mr. Registrar, 3D00731 would receive what number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1836.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, no objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1836 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cvrk, when we discussed professional training, schooling and courses taken by members of special police units, can you tell us whether there was any sort of international cooperation in existence as well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: As far as it was possible under the wartime circumstances, efforts were made to draw upon the knowledge of other special police forces in the region and worldwide and to [French on English channel] -- these courses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let's turn to a different topic now which is the engagement of special police -- [French on English channel].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are now moving five seconds English, five seconds French, approximately. I like both languages equally but not at the same time. I don't know what caused the problem but -- because it's not usual that it switches again and again. Is there any technical problem behind it? If not, let's give it a try. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to call up document D1090.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvrk, these are instructions dating from May 1993 made by the head of the special police department, Mr. Mladen Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're waiting for the document to appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the preamble the following is stated: In view of the new proposal for the internal structure of the Ministry of Interior and in relation to the scope of work of the special police, I hereby issue the following instructions concerning the existing conditions of work which are to temporarily regulate the relations within the special police force among members who conduct combat tasks in the field. Subsequently, the instructions concerning joint forces follow. To your knowledge, Mr. Cvrk, prior to 1993, were special police units organised as part of joint forces whenever major operations needed to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: There were, indeed, several actions where, in the area of responsibility of various police administrations where order was disrupted, such actions were taken by joint forces. In 1991 to a lesser extent and in 1992. The document we have before us is the one where, around Operation Maslenica, the engagement of joint forces was affirmed in this way and became the model according to which members of various police administrations were assembled for a specific task that they were supposed to carry out for the benefit of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, then, Mr. Cvrk, that up until 1995 and Operation Storm, this model of assembling joint forces had already been well established; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Yes, it was a customary method of work, where heads of police administrations were informed of elements of their units being placed at the disposal for the ministry to conduct any of the tasks which were carried out at the state level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up document P554, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The internal organisation of the joint forces thus formed was based on guide-lines and orders. Before you is an order whereby the staff of the joint forces of the special police was set up on the 23rd of July, 1995, shortly before Operation Storm. Can you briefly tell us how such joint forces worked internally, in terms of the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: The chain of command was specifically defined by individual orders, depending on the task given. The chain of command, or the structure of command, was well known to all those who were involved in a particular action, regardless of what their organic unit was. The unit I was in command of could, up to 50 per cent, be detached and dispatched for specific missions, be it to hold the separation line between us and the enemy, being to make sure that the agreements reached concerning the demarcation line are to be honoured. Such orders defined the strength of individual units and specific locations of the staff of the joint forces, who was in charge of the staff, and who was in charge of the particular line to be defended, or whatever the task was; in other words, who was tasked with what along the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that specifically your unit, the special police unit of the Zagreb police administration, could, at some point, be deprived of up to 50 per cent of its men for the purposes of such actions of joint forces. The remaining men remained within the authority of the Zagreb police administration. Did they fall under the chain of command of the joint forces? And I mean the policemen who stayed behind as part of the special police unit of the police administration.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: The special police unit of the Zagreb police administration had a clearly defined task in terms of the deployment of its Rapid Reaction Force, which covered the state and administrative seats, international representatives, embassies, and was specialised in combat against all manner of crime, including terrorism and dealing with hostage situations. The policemen who stayed behind in the police administration were directly subordinated to the head of the police administration and did not come under the chain of command of the joint police forces tasked with specific state-level missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The joint forces staff, which was set up in late July of 1995, was set up because of the imminent participation of the police forces in Operation Storm; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: I believe so. However, it is also likely that this order also served the purpose of setting up police forces for Operation Summer, Ljeto, to man the separation line opposite the enemy in the Military Districts of Gospic and Split. I know that an intervention unit was set up for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, the joint forces themselves and the staff were set up as part of the plans for Mount Velebit, is that right, and were deployed there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Elements of your special police unit of the Zagreb police administration were also part of these joint police forces? And I'm referring to the combat action that the police units were a part of in the course of Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up document D543.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvrk, I will show you the order issued by the Main Staff of the Croatian Army, which, in fact, launched Operation Storm, and which issued the special police with the specific task. We can see under item 1 that the MUP special forces were given their axis of attack. Under item 2, it was stated that the operation should be carried out in two phases over the course of three days. In the first phase they were supposed to use their own artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's turn to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And they were supposed to cut off the roadway between Gospic and Gracac. Mr. Cvrk, what was the role you played in Operation Storm as the commander of the special police unit of the Zagreb police administration?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: In addition to the general tasks that all the forces were given, in terms of the implementation of the military and police Operation Storm, as I stated in my statement, I was the commander of the fourth auxiliary axis which was supposed to tie up most of the forces and was supposed to carry out the tasks that we were given by the Main Staff of the Croatian Army. There were several units to be deployed along this auxiliary axis. We were supposed to reach the Gospic-Gracac roadway in the general area of the village of Ruke, thus securing most of the forces and make sure that they reached the Celavac repeater and the Prezid feature, as well as everything else that was ordered in this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As part of preparations for combat activity, did you receive specific information concerning the enemy who was supposed to be engaged? Their strength, deployment, units, and such-like?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: During preparations for Operation Storm, and the dates are the 28th, the 29th of July, thereabout, every commander was handed maps which had their axis of deployment plotted in. They each received their set of tasks which indicated the general areas they were supposed to take. And alongside the maps and tasks, we received intelligence concerning the enemy, their strength, forces, deployment, deployment of their artillery, and the location of other relevant targets. We needed all of that documentation in order to be able to launch attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has already received evidence to that effect. The operation itself started in the morning at around 5.00 on the 4th. The axis that were in command of, namely the fourth auxiliary axis, what sort of progress did you make along that axis and what were the tasks that you achieved on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: As I already said previously, at the auxiliary axis where I was the commander, the anti-terrorist unit, as well as the special police unit of the Primorsko Gorinska area were deployed, the majority of the unit that I commanded was resubordinated to the third auxiliary axis, with Mr. Cindric, and the reserve forces were the special unit of the Krapina and Zagorje police administration. In the first day, we achieved all the tasks that we had been issued with. We reached the roads in the Ruke village sector. We secured the site. We also took the combat position and we prepared for many days of fighting with the enemy, if necessary, because the main task of this position was that it was expected that introduction of new forces would move through this area, as well as reinforcement for the enemy at the positions of Mali Alan and Celavac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you say that you reached in the Ruke village sector, why was this position strategically important, in relation to the road leading from Gospic towards Gracac, and further on in the direction of the cross-roads with Otric and then later, Bruvno and so on. What was the strategic importance of this road?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: We cannot talk about strategic importance but this was a tactical point because, by cutting off this road, additional logistical support was cut off for the forces that were holding the front line, and the forces on the mountain of Velebit were not on lines that would be turned into trenches and trench warfare, but they were just holding certain local points or fortified places. The conditions were difficult and the aim was to gain the upper hand and to disperse the enemy as much as possible, to cut him off in as main points as possible, and to let him know that by introducing so many units and men and by covering military targets with precise artillery fire, that we were determined to achieve our goals. And this is how we managed to achieve what we needed to do so that reinforcements could not be introduced behind our own forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And the terrain across which you advanced from Velebit towards another place, how densely populated was it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: It can be noted that the area of Licko Polje is one of the most sparsely populated areas in Croatia. If we talk about populated places, in the axis of advance, there were just hamlets, a few houses scattered here and there, so it is only occasionally populated area, very sparsely populated, because people keep cattle in this area and there were not too many populated places on the axis of the advance of special police units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, neither my colleagues nor myself do fully understand the relevance of what you are asking now, whether it was of strategic importance where this unit was, or tactical importance. It is totally unclear to us. So if you'd please focus your questions in such a way that we understand how the answers could assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will try to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cvrk, during the combat advance on the first and second days of the Operation Storm, did you come across any civilians? Did you have any combat contacts in the area that included any civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: One should say that the area of Velebit is unpopulated; that was where the special police was. And on the first day, after we achieved the combat results by making it impossible for the enemy to reinforce his units on our axis, on the first day, it was practically impossible to come across any civilians because of the terrain. And on the second day, when we went further in the direction of Gospic, I could say that the space was almost completely empty, because the area of Medak pocket was a depression which, without further advance, could easily be completely surrounded. So it was logical that the enemy, together with the population and everything they could take with themselves, withdrew from there so that there were practically no civilians left in the area through which we advanced from the village of Ruke towards Lovinac, Sveti Rok, and to the west, that is to say, the north-west, in the direction of Gospic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the information that you received before the operation, did you learn anything about the enemy formations which were standing, so to speak, on the other side, facing you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, that was part of the intelligence that we received, as part of the order for carrying out our combat operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the document D435.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvrk, I will show you now a document which is already in evidence. It is a document issued by the commander of the 9th Motorised Gracac Brigade of the Serbian Army of Krajina. Let me first ask you if you ever had a chance to see this document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: I saw this document during the preparation for my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I meant before that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Not before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will just point out to you some information contained in this document and then I will ask you to place that in the context of your observations on the ground. First of all, it is mentioned here that the command of the 9th Brigade received on the 3rd of August, the day before Operation Storm, around 2350 hours, the information that an attack of Ustasha forces was expected. And then it says that the attack was launched at around 5.00 a.m. in the region of Mali Alan, and that heavy artillery fire was launched on the Gospic-Medak axis. And that the forces had broken through along this axis, and that, as a consequence of that, the brigade had to withdraw, together with the men, and the equipment. On page 2 of this document, there is a listing of all the combat equipment and machinery with which the brigade withdrew. Mr. Cvrk, the tempo of your advance had to be great in this operation. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Yes. It can be confirmed that, as we took control of all this area on foot, then the tempo, as we used few vehicles, was really great.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And during the advance, did you have any contacts with the enemy units which were withdrawing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: I can note that on the first day we had intensive combat contact with them and that was continued until we reached the internationally recognised border between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document it is stated that the brigade of the Serbian Army of Krajina managed to pull out practically all its machinery, except only if there was not enough fuel. So we can see that they had tanks and trucks and so on. And on the third page, in the conclusion, it is stated that the brigade, on approval of its superior command, had to begin organised withdrawal and the deployment was such that they also secured the withdrawal of the civilian population and their own forces and equipment. Mr. Cvrk, this is military speak, so I would ask you if could you please comment on this formulation. What does it mean that, by its combat deployment, the brigade secured the withdrawal of its own forces and civilian population?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: The commander of the 9th Gracac Brigade wanted to sum up the total combat operations of the unit that he commanded by this document and he described the first day of combat operations and of the advance of special police. And by his combat deployment, he was securing the withdrawal of his forces, equipment and civilian population on the later days which means that he would leave parts of his unit behind the main group of forces so that they would have enough time to withdraw the population as well as the equipment and the members of the entire brigade to Petrovac, which is mentioned there if I'm not mistaken, which means that it was a withdrawal into Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And in the pulling out of the enemy units and your advance, were there any combat contacts between you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Certainly. When we achieved the first results on the first day, the special police, in accordance with further orders, was engaged on several axes and it also tried to take part of various areas, mainly the main rows [as interpreted], and then setting up communications for the needs of logistics and to enable the introduction of reinforcement, if necessary, and once we achieved our final goal, that is to say, when we reached the state border, during all these movements by artillery or infantry weapons or whether it was attacks on the special police units that was going on throughout all of these days [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was the axis that, after you took control of the road and the town of Gracac, that the special police units advanced along?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: There were several orders. We call them orders D plus 1, D plus 2, of D plus 3 orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for reference to the Chamber, D plus 1, D plus 2, and D plus 3 orders have been admitted as documents D550, then D552, and D322.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Cvrk.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: In accordance with these orders, after we achieved the main goals on our first day, on the second day, we went on to liberate the Gracac. Another part of the forces linked up with the forces of the Military District of Gospic, in Gospic. Then, in the evening, as far as I remember, they continued their advance towards Otric. I think, Prezid was also successfully liberated. And already on the second day, in the evening, we advanced with a part of our forces towards Bruvno. On the third day, in accordance with the order, we went towards Udbina, from Bruvno, and that was the auxiliary axis, while the main part of the forces went from Bruvno towards Gornji and Donji Lapac, and finally, in the area of Kulen Vakuf, it reached the state and administrative border, that is to say, the border between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So to say everything briefly, how the special police units advanced during Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did your unit and did you personally have the chance to move through the town of Gracac during your advance during the Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: The unit that I commanded, on the second day, in accordance with the order D plus 1, was engaged in the direction of Otric, but at the end of this day, a command post of special police was established in the town of Gracac, and for the purpose of coordination I was invited there.
