So I passed through the town of Gracac several times in order to pass on the tasks or to receive tasks, and also on the occasion when the police station in Gracac was opened. So I was present in the town of Gracac on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And as far as you remember, Mr. Cvrk, to what extent was it visible that there was any damage in the town of Gracac as a result of combat operations while you were passing through the town?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: It was visible that, due to artillery fire, against cross-roads and some legitimate military targets such as the police station and the command of the brigade, that there had been some combat activity and some machinery was abandoned. It was possible that it was useless or that it couldn't be pulled out because of the quick advance of special police units towards Gracac, so that the impression was of an abandoned town which was in the zone of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvrk, you said that you noticed some damage on the police station, as well as on the building where the Gracac brigade had been accommodated. Do you remember what sort of building that was? I'm talking about the command building.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Well, not the command building itself, no, because Gracac was not part of the tasks I was charged with. However, the centre where the -- subsequently the command of the special police force was set up and where the police station was, I have a pretty good recollection of that, despite the time that lapsed in between, in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How would you assess the degree of damage to the buildings in Gracac, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Most of the damage was inflicted by artillery shrapnel. I passed along the main road in the settlement, and there were several buildings aflame, probably due to the same reason. And laterally, where there was some family homes, there were bullet marks as well. They were bullet-riddled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your unit next proceeded in the direction of Bruvno; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Yes. That was day D plus 3, since on day plus 2, most of the forces moving along Gornji Donji Vapac [as interpreted] toward Kulen Vakuf gathered there, whereas another batch of forces headed from the area of Bruvno. When we reached Bruvno that morning, we were supposed to move in the direction of Udbina and link up with the forces of the Gospic Military District there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After day three of Storm, what were the specific tasks given to your unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, that was day D plus 3, when the enemy forces regrouped yet again and reached Kulen Vakuf, from where they opened artillery fire on us. They also used tank fire. The task was to group forces and the -- we received the orders from the special police units staff, so we're talking about the 8th, when we were supposed to link up with the forces from Gospic. On that day, we were replaced by a military unit, which deployed in our area of activity. In other words, we completed our task, reached the state border between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereupon we received orders to withdraw from the area since we have completed our mission within Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Members of the units you were in command of and, if you know, other units, how did they move about the front line? Were vehicles organised for that purpose, or did they walk?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: As for the movement of special police units, initially, we walked. We had to traverse a ragged, mountainous area, and a kilometre into the area, we were moving along a slope of some 45 degrees slant. The area didn't have any roads, and we had to cross the Mali Alan pass. We carried some artillery pieces. We had a -- several APCs. Roughly those supply routes, Gracac, Obrovac, had to be made passable, and on days D plus 1, plus 2, plus 3, we could use the vehicles we had, our own vehicles, and they were enough for 40 per cent of our men, 45 to 50 per cent of our men. However, for the rest, for most of the operation, we walked in a skirmish line and we walked, where possible, along the roadways which were along our axis anyway, and, of course, wherever we expected that we could possibly engage enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What were the vehicles used by the special police in their advancement for the transportation of personnel and assets?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Different types of vans which could seat some eight to nine men, all the way to lorries which could carry equipment, ammunition, logistic support, and could also tow some of the rocket and artillery pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was the extent of the travel that had to be done by the special police forces all the way from Mount Velebit, where they started, to Kulen Vakuf, where they ultimately stopped?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: The pace at which progress was made was some 20 to 30 kilometres. So in all these days, we covered some 60 to 70 -- 60 to 80 kilometres. But that's an approximation of the pace at which special police forces could advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You personally and your unit, did you reach Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Yes, I personally came to Donji Lapac in order to report on our linking up at Udbina with units of the Gospic Military District, the 9th Guards Brigade. I reported on this. The rocket artillery battery was part of the joint forces, which originally belonged to my units and had been detached and deployed there for combat purposes. And I think I was on the -- it was on the 7th of August, late in the evening, that I was in Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was the situation like in Lapac as you got there on the 7th of August, in the evening hours?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: It was quite obvious that a high degree of combat activity had taken place there. The command building and the police station had received several direct hits. The hotel, the local hotel was on fire, as well as a vehicle which had been carrying some assets. It had been hit and was on fire. So there was plenty to see. What could also be seen was that the special police forces were deployed deep behind the lines in the direction of Kulen Vakuf, in the direction of the village of Boricevac. They were deploying along the state border, as I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Lapac?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Until night-fall. I spent some time there with the men from the battery that I referred to. I had taken orders for further activities, and, unless I'm mistaken, I was invited to a coordination meeting of all special police unit commanders at the staff on the following morning, at some 10.00 or 11.00 in the morning. And then I returned on the same day, in the evening, under enemy artillery fire, to where my unit was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The next day was the 8th of August. What was the task to be carried out by your unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: On the 8th of August, an analysis was made of attacks carried out and results achieved. The front units stopped which meant that all the units behind had to stop as well, and they had to take stock of what they had done. At the end of the coordination meeting, most of the units start receiving orders to deploy back to their organic units and this, in fact, took place on the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was the axis along which your unit was disengaged back to the Zagreb police administration from the general area of Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: I can't be sure but I think we went via Udbina, Plitvice, on to Zagreb. But I'm not positive about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When did you, in fact, reach your organic unit in Zagreb, along with your men?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: We returned to Zagreb in the early afternoon hours of the 9th of August. We have a record of that, since we passed along the main square in Zagreb, so there has to be a record of that somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to other elements of the joint forces after the 8th or the 9th of August, when the end of Operation Storm was formally announced?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: To my knowledge, most of the units were -- were disengaged, one by one, in succession; and, as far as I remember, until the end of the day, and I'm referring to the 9th of August, all of us had left the general area of Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up D1103 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Once the joint forces had done their job, their part of the job in the military/police Operation Storm, there followed a period which was marked by some other activity, and the Trial Chamber heard about this, the sweeping of terrain. You can see the order of the 10th of August, 1995, here, which was issued by the chief of the Main Staff, General Cervenko, according to which the MUP special police units are ordered to carry out the mopping up and occupy the Petrova Gora area under the orders of General Mladen Markac. Can you tell us what the location of Petrova Gora is in relation to where the joint forces were active in Operation Storm? Is it part of Operation South [as interpreted], or is it outside of that area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: As far as I know, the area lies outside of Sector South. Unless I'm mistaken, it should come under the Karlovac Military District. However, since we, as policemen, were not much concerned with the boundaries of the Military Districts, I can tell you that it was to the north of Sector South where we carried out our tasks during Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was your unit involved in the sweeping operation of Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: I personally, and most of the unit's members were involved in the sweeping operation at Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This isn't something I have already asked you but, Mr. Cvrk, do you know what was the total number of special policemen who were part of the joint forces during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: According to the reports I saw, I think that there were roughly 2.200 men involved in Operation Storm, and then subsequently perhaps some fresh forces and logistics men may have been brought in which may have caused the figure to rise to 2500.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How long did the sweeping operation at Petrova Gora last?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: As far as I remember, not more than ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Following the action which involved the participation of the special police as part of the joint forces, what happened next? Were these forces returned to their bases, or were they subsequently re-engaged in actions of sorts?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: The equipment and the composition of the special police forces were such that we were a highly mobile unit and were able to cross the country from one end to the next very rapidly and were able to carry out the most complex of combat tasks. There were several such actions which ensued after Operation Storm which were prevalently conditioned by the intelligence received and the possible infiltration of enemy groups, the leftover enemy soldiers, as well as by the high -- or, rather, the vast territory of the liberated area which had to be searched for straggling enemy soldiers which might cause -- pose a risk. According to the -- this was done pursuant to the requests of the Ministry of the Interior or of the Main Staff of the Croatian Army. The special police units were used in such operations, and they were, like this one, termed "sweeping operations," in order to stabilise the situation on the ground and to allow for a smooth restoration of authority in the area, in the liberated area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could now please see the document D561.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tying up with what you just told us, Mr. Cvrk, I will show you a document in which the chief of Main Staff, General Zvonimir Cervenko, on the 21st of August, ordered that the terrain is to be searched and mopped up. And in the introduction he says that some outlaw groups remained in the area next to the state border, as well as in some areas and facilities that have not yet been searched. And then he says that the purpose units of the MUP will do that, and that the chief of Main Staff makes the commands of the Military Districts and garrisons responsible for submitting information on the possible presence of enemy groups in the area. After this order, issued on 21st August 1995, the search of the terrain followed in the area which was liberated during Operation Storm. Did your unit also participate in this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Yes. One part of our unit was engaged, I think it was between 120 and 150 members, during this operation which we called, if I remember properly, Oluja-Obrecun [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please see the document D562 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvrk, I will show you a report on the search of terrain carried out for the 21st of August, which was submitted by Colonel General Mladen Markac to the Main Staff of the Croatian Army, to General Cervenko, where, under item 3 he mentions that the special police unit of the Zagreb police administration, with 130 of its members, took part in the search of the terrain and that the following materiel and technical equipment such as ammunition for mortars and ammunition for infantry weapons were found. Mr. Cvrk, during these search operations, can you tell me briefly what kind of the terrain was this in the newly liberated areas that were part of the so-called former Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: This was terrain that was mountainous, very difficult to pass through and this report only confirms some of the data that we had previously, and that during the combat contact we had during Operation Oluja, whether it was the HVO units or the special police units, that we searched the terrain and found many pieces of abandoned machinery, as noted in this report. In addition to that, in this area, in some of the hamlets that we passed through and everywhere else, there were some civilians whom we recorded, and fairly quickly we would establish their status and then we would direct them to receive assistance or to report themselves to police stations or to UNHCR, which was already active, so some people were registered, some were not, so that they would realise their rights to be granted assistance. These were mostly elderly people who had been left behind and who were mostly very old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As for the contacts with the civilian population that you found during the searches of the terrain, did you receive any instructions about those from your superiors?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: We had very precise instructions about the rights of the individual, the international law of war, and, on the final days of Operation Storm, we also had specific instructions about the international personnel who were deployed on the ground, what authority they had and how we could assist them to perform their duties. Even though we had numerous combat contacts between straggling enemy forces and our own forces, and even though we had wounded members, even 15 days after Operation Storm had de facto been concluded, this was a very strict task for the special police because its purpose was to establish whether the area that had been liberated was clear of enemy soldiers, first of all, and also what was the total number of the population that was possibly left in the area. So clearly we had to register these people and inform the special police sector about this in daily reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please see the document P576.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvrk, I will show you a report on a completed search of the terrain for the day the 25th of August, 1995, submitted also by Colonel General Mladen Markac to the assistant minister for special police. It says here that the search had been conducted in which area, and somewhere in the middle of the document or thereabouts it says that in the village of Pasici, a suspect male was found and was delivered to crime police for further investigation. It is also mentioned that in the village of Grubor, during the search, eight to ten enemy soldiers were observed, that there was an exchange of fire and that the result was the death of Djuro Karanovic, 45 years of age and residing in Belgrade, who was armed with a sniper rifle, and that, after that, Stevan Karanovic who was also armed with a semi-automatic rifle was arrested, and that two other unidentified females and two elderly men, Milos Grubor and Jovo Grubor, were also killed. Mr. Cvrk, did your unit and you, yourself, did you know anything about the events in the village of Grubor on that day, that is to say, the 25th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: As one can see from this report, the unit was engaged on a quite different axis but the general information that I had, of course, I heard that there was some activity in the village of Grubori, but I absolutely do not remember and do not know all the details in connection with this because I was issued other tasks and I was not member of the command of the sector that had to carry out these activities and control the activities of all of us and all the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Further on it says here that during the search in the villages on the initial position, 52 civilians have been registered -- 54 civilians, that is to say, and eventually it says, at the end, that the Croatian civilian population has not yet established contact with the civilians who were found. And the list of civilians who were found was made by members of UNCRO. Do you remember that on the occasion of this operation, on the 25th, that these 54 civilians were found or was it not on your axis? Did you learn anything about this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly but, generally, on all of these days, there were situations when we would come across the persons who had remained in the area, whether persons who had been registered by UNCRO or persons who had registered by reporting themselves to the police stations that had been set up in the area. So these were three main ways for civilians to establish their status in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please see P579.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvrk, for your information, this is a report on the task for the 26th of August, for special police, also submitted by Colonel General Mladen Markac, wherein it is stated that in the village Knezevici civilians were found and registered. And in the village of Karanovac, six civilians were found. And then in the village of Ridjane, persons were found and registered by the regular police from the MUP. In addition to registering these persons and submitting that to the regular police of the MUP, did special police have any other obligations in connection with the civilians found during the search of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: No. According to my recollection, the obligation to the civilians, which included all kinds of people, people who couldn't move, who were in need of medical assistance, so sometimes we didn't even have to go to the police stations, and in some hamlets and some positions where we found these elderly people were in areas where roads were very bad. There were sometimes only paths and these were places difficult to access, so we would register these people. We needed complete registration of everyone, but that was not really our job to do anything after that. That was a duty of the authorities on the ground, whether it was the police or whoever communicated with the forces of UNCRO along the axis where we were advancing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the document P2379 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Following up on this, you will see a report on tasks carried out on the 27th of August. Again, it is a search of the terrain. And if we move on to page 2 of this report, we will see in paragraph 4, that two unregistered civilians were also found in the village of Silici [phoen]; in the village were Borovici, another two unidentified civilians; in the village of Kukolj [phoen], it's the same thing. And then around 1200, in the place Kavacevica Stanove [phoen], an attack was launched from fire-arms by a member of the enemy army who was then arrested and delivered to military police. Do you remember, Mr. Cvrk, whether there were any contacts with straggling enemy soldiers during these operations of the search of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: One can see from this report and from the fact that some members of the special police unit were wounded because of such contacts, it's evident that there were such contacts, even 20 or 30 or even more days after the conclusion of the Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: All the search operations were carried out in Sector South where formally Operation Storm was launched. How long did they last? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: It is certain that they lasted in accordance with orders, and depending on the coordination of the forces of the special police and the Croatian Army, and after the conclusion of pulling out of combat equipment, and once it was established that there shouldn't be many more straggling enemy soldiers left behind, then these search operations stopped. And I think that -- when I say all this, I'm talking about mid-September or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please see 65 ter 02264 now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, just before we move to the next, I missed perhaps something. You said, Mr. Cvrk, As you can see from this report and from the fact that some members of the special police units were wounded because of such contacts, I'm just trying to find, where in this document, we find wounded special police officers, but I may have missed it. Could you help me out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it is not mentioned in this document but it is fact that one of our colleagues was wounded in this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us further details.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, I'm sure that it was Mr. Labrovic, but as for the exact date on which it happened and the circumstances, I would have to refresh my memory, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please see 65 ter 02264.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The document that you see on the screen, Mr. Cvrk, is a document informing about the planned activities of the joint special police forces on 8 September 1995, and Colonel General Mladen Markac informs about this. The area is that of Plitvice, where, if there are any straggling sabotage and terrorist groups, then they should be found. And it is mentioned then what are the axes but this is the general area of Plitvice. Mr. Cvrk, did your unit take part in searching the terrain in the area of Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For orientation purposes only, can you tell us whether the area of Plitvice is within Sector South, in the newly liberated territory?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: I didn't pay much heed to that type of delineation. But if you're asking me whether the area of Plitvice is without the sector in which the special police forces under my command pursued activities in the initial days of Operation Storm, then my question is -- my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I seek clarification when it was said that, When you're asking me if the area is without the sector, did you mean outside the sector?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning my answer, I wanted to say that this was outside or without the sector in which the special police forces pursued their activities in the initial days of Operation Storm, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that answer. Ms. Mahindaratne, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1837.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to remind the Court that concerning the search of the terrain in the area of Plitvice, there are other documents which I would kindly seek to tender, or would you rather have me go through each and every of those documents with the witness? These are 65 ter documents 00503, 00515, and the sequence of documents goes up to the 13th of September. The last of the documents speaks of the search of the terrain around Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can go through them. I'll make it a brief exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was not asking it. If there's no objections against bar tabling these documents, Ms. Mahindaratne, then the Chamber would expect, as usual, a joint filing in which we are informed about the relevance and specific portions to pay attention to. Now, if you say, So therefore I leave it your hands. At the same time, I'm looking at the clock, Mr. Mikulicic, I think this witness was announced for two sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will finish within five to ten minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we can continue before the break until you've finished, concluded your --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can easily go through one or two documents on that topic as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I leave it in your hands --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as long as you finish within five or ten minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask for the 65 ter document 00515 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It is an information on the planned activities for the 10th of August submitted by Colonel General Mladen Markac in the wider area of Plitvice, where the joint forces, on the 10th of August, were supposed to carry out certain activities between 7.00 a.m. and 7.00 p.m. The activities concerned were actually terrain searches. Does this tally with what you can recall, Mr. Cvrk, concerning the searches in the area of Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Certainly. These are standard daily reports, daily informations that we were provided with indicating directions and areas that were supposed to be sweeped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1838.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next I would kindly ask for D566 to be shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The document we are about to see, Mr. Cvrk, has already been admitted. It is a joint report on the completed task of the search in the broader area of the National Park Plitvice of the 12th of September, 1995, in which mention is made of the fact that the terrain of the national park of Plitvice was searched, covering 22 by 40 kilometres. The total area was 880 square kilometres. It says that, daily, members of the special police searched some 25 kilometres of terrain in skirmish lines at distances between 1500 metres between each member. The goal was to create a secure environment to protect property. On the second page of this document, it is stated that no straggling enemy forces were located and that, in total, eight corpses of uniformed unidentified soldiers were found and the corpses were already in a state of decay or putrefaction. It is also stated that several elderly persons were found and taken care of in several villages, and that their citizenship status was resolved accordingly. It is also stated that 16 B and H nationals were found who had illegally crossed the state border, and sporting individual items of clothing that belonged to uniforms. On the next page, we have mines and explosives of which a certain amount was found, and mention is also made that the bed of the lake that was in the area was searched by the special police members who were scuba divers. This is the concerning the sweeping of the terrain. Were members of your unit included in these speciality searches such as the search of the lake -- of the lakes, actually, at Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: I believe that our frogmen basically came from the anti-terrorist unit of Lucko. We did have a scuba diver for the needs of the Zagreb police administration, in order to extract bodies of casualties or to search certain water beds of which there were many in our police administration territory. But at that time, that speciality group was attached to the anti-terrorist unit of Lucko, as well as to the administrations in Split and Rijeka. I believe therefore that their personnel was used to search the Plitvice lakes. When we arrived there, it was widely believed that the barriers separating the individual levels of the lakes were mined in order to disturb the further flow of the river, and this was supposed to be ascertained by the frogmen of the special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In conclusion, I would ask for D1105. After the searches were carried out in Plitvice, on the 11th of September, a new order arrived from the chief of the Main Staff, Mr. Cervenko, by virtue of which it is ordered that the special forces of the MUP, amounting to about 2.000 men, should be sent to the southern theatre, in keeping with their deployment plan. Two questions concerning this. Which part of the Croatian territory does this refer to when the southern theatre is mentioned; and did any of your units members take part in this new task issued by the commander of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: I am certain that a unit I commanded was also encompassed this. This is about the line of separation along the state borders of Croatia and Bosnia. If I am not mistaken, it was also a border to Montenegro and Serbia, and the general area of the town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You were subordinated to Mr. Markac, who was assistant interior minister for the special police during a certain period of time. In a few words, can you tell us what was your relationship to him and what is your opinion of him as a commander and as an ordinary person?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: After my arrival in the special police and in particular after I was appointed commander of the Alpha Unit, I kept permanent contact with the assistant minister for the interior, Mr. Mladen Markac. I can tell you about Mr. Markac as my wartime commander that, by virtue of his activities and his attempts to be specific in terms of organisational and personnel needs as well as any other needs to ensure the work of the special police, he tried to use his influence to create the conditions within the ministry so that those forces could be trained, that they could act properly, be equipped -- equipped properly, and that the entire special police structure be put in place. I believe by virtue of those actions, by creating the necessary preconditions as well as the implementing of systematic training as well as issuing -- by issuing direct orders, and creating conditions in which we were on a par in terms of equipment with our enemy, he created favourable conditions for work in the special police forces in general, as well in the overall context of armed forces in Croatia. I believe much is due to him, because he achieved much through the Ministry of the Interior. I consider him a highly moral person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cvrk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will have a break and resume at five minutes to 1.00. And after the break, Mr. Cvrk, cross-examination will start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, apologies for the late start. I don't know who is on his feet for the.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we have no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions. Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you may proceed. Mr. Cvrk, you will be cross-examined by Ms. Mahindaratne. Ms. Mahindaratne is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Cvrk.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you, when you were interviewed on behalf of the Defence team for Mr. Markac, you were interviewed by Mr. Franjo Djurica and Anto Soljic. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And Mr. Djurica Franjo was the chief of the police coordinators appointed to OZ Sector South, in August 1995, in the aftermath of Operation Storm. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And he held that position until December 1995; are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the details, since Mr. Franjo Djurica was connected to the police sector of the Ministry of the Interior through his work. We cooperated at a later date on the peaceful reintegration of Eastern Slavonia. I am not aware of what his duties were when he was in charge of coordinating special police units.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You referred to coordinating special police units. Did you mean to say coordinating police units, because Mr. Franjo Djurica was a police coordinator attached to the Ministry of Interior, isn't that correct, he was not part of the special police? I wonder whether you made a mistake when you mentioned the word "special police."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: If we're talking about 1995 and the position of the coordinator on behalf of the police, that particular position had predominantly to do with the forces of the newly set up police stations in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's the clarification I sought. And were you aware that, in fact, the police coordinators in charge of the Knin area, Mr. Baric and Mr. Buhin, in fact reported to Mr. Djurica; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: I can't confirm this with any degree of certainty, since I was busy with the work on the ground. It was the sector of the special police which dealt with police coordination. We were one of the elements. I wasn't active in the special police sector in order for me to be able to confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you aware that Mr. Djurica himself is on the list of witnesses for the Defence for Mr. Markac?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: As far as this trial is concerned and my appearance, I was contacted a year and a half ago, in order to give my statement, together with these individuals who were signed here. Now, as for the witnesses who would appear on behalf of General Markac, I'm aware only of the information that was available to me, and I did not hear that Mr. Djurica was on the list of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, the second person who interviewed you, Mr. Anto Soljic, was the head of the inner control branch of the special police during that the whole of 1995, going into 1996; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: That's correct. Mr. Anto Soljic was the chief of the internal control of the special police sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And isn't it right that the internal control of the special police sector was responsible for monitoring and reporting on the discipline of the special police units to the special police sector command?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Internal control gathered information about the overall activities of the unit, primarily, those relating to discipline, and processed the information for the purposes of the special police sector and for the purposes of a report that was sent to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you aware that the internal control, in fact, submitted reports of discipline within the units, in fact, to the special police sector, that is, Mr. Markac and Mr. Sacic? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: From the experience I have as commander of the unit, the internal control did not have any major bearing on the state of affairs with regard to discipline. They were mostly involved, like in Operation Storm, in gathering counter-intelligence information of units and information on the enemy in general, and it had to do with putting together intelligence operatives. So these were the duties that the internal control of the special police sector had, as far as I'm able to remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvrk, I have a problem trying to understand. Your previous answer was this: Internal control gathered information about the overall activities of the unit, primarily those relating to discipline, and processed the information for the purpose of the special police sector and for the purposes of a report that was sent to the Ministry of the Interior. But thereafter, you now say: From the experience I have as commander of the unit, the internal control did not have any major bearing on the state of affairs with regard to discipline. Perhaps I'm misunderstanding what you're trying to say. Now, is it correct that internal control branch was a section of the special police that monitored discipline within the units and maintained records and reported on the state of discipline to the special police sector command? And when I use the word "sector command," I refer to Mr. Markac and Mr. Sacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think he has answered that already, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, I was just waiting for the French translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. He has answered the question and just because she doesn't like the way he has answered the question, doesn't mean that she gets to ask it again. There were two separate questions. The first question was on line -- page 68, line 20, she asked him a specific question about internal control of the special police and he answered the specific question. The problem was -- the problem is she answered -- asked a separate question in which he gave an answer which was also correct, and I think the Prosecution is confused as to which answer compares to which question. And I think the person -- the witness has answered the question both times and to ask it again I think is repetitive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether the answer to the second question was correct or not, Mr. Kuzmanovic, I wouldn't know yet. The problem -- let me just re-read it. Yes, the problem arises because your first question was a question about facts and the second question was about a judgement. And that, at the same time, Mr. Kuzmanovic, is a key to the solution. Ms. Mahindaratne, you may ask once whether -- that you have some difficulties in reconciling your judgement with the factual answer, but, then, you have to move on. And, of course, you can address the matter in other ways. But that is the problem if a witness of fact is asked to give his judgement, whether it has any bearing is typically a matter of judgement, that that creates these kind of situations and I therefore urge you to -- to, as much as possible, stick to the facts. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvrk, if you could just answer this question: Were you aware that the inner control branch submitted reports on the state of discipline of the special police units to the special police sector command?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: In terms of making annual reports on disciplinary proceedings and in terms of the work of operatives, well, they did process all the data concerning these units and included it in the intelligence analysis that the special police sector produced. In addition to this, we had monthly reports that we made concerning all the activities taken by a given special police unit within its area of responsibility over a 30-day period. It is possible that, alongside this, there was an uninterrupted analysis made of all things that were done in that sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you, as head of a special police unit in Zagreb, report to Mr. Soljic on discipline within your unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: No. I was responsible for my line of work to the assistant minister, to Mr. Markac, the head of the special police department, and to the -- to Mr. Sacic, the head of the special police sector to whom I addressed the report and for whose benefit I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, there was some discussion about discipline within the special police. Now, are you aware that, if -- before that. You testified that as the head of the special police unit, you were responsible for initiating disciplinary measures against members of your unit when they committed breaches of discipline. Now, isn't that correct that if you, as the -- the commander of the special police unit in Zagreb, did not initiate disciplinary measures against a member who had committed a breach, General Markac had the authority to directly order you to do so. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: As I've already explained, there were minor and major breaches of discipline. The -- it is set out that the minister may confer his authority to chiefs of police administrations on this score, which he did. Then the chiefs of police administrations, in turn, conferred this power on to heads of certain departments. The Zagreb police administration, as a whole, had conferred upon me the power to initiate disciplinary proceedings, to take disciplinary measures against those members of my unit who committed minor breaches of discipline, or to initiate there disciplinary proceedings be launched in the first instance within the police administration and within the ministry in the second instance. Throughout my career, I had never been faced with a situation where Mr. Mladen Markac or the special police sector called upon me to initiate disciplinary proceedings against a member of the special police for a minor or a major breach of discipline.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Although you have not come across such situations, are you aware that General Markac this the authority to do so, that he could, in fact, order a commander of a special police unit to initiate discipline against a member of that unit? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: This may be so, but only where the sector of the special police itself was concerned and its employees, the helicopter unit which was part of the special police sector and the Lucko Anti-Terrorist Unit which was also part of the special police sector. It was only in these cases that this could have done directly. But I am not aware of any other such cases involving units that were under police administrations. We were the ones who were directly responsible for discipline.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may have I document P610, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cvrk --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, I'm a bit confused by the last answer and I would like to seek clarification before we continue. You said only in relation to those units you specifically mentioned, that is, the helicopter unit and the Lucko Unit, that it was only in these cases that this could have done directly. Now, I understood from Ms. Mahindaratne's question that she asked you whether Mr. Markac could instruct you to take disciplinary measures against someone of your subordinates, which I would consider indirect approach. That is, Mr. Markac -- you told us he never did but that at least in theory, Mr. Markac instructed you to take disciplinary measures. Now, is that what you had on your mind when you said this was only -- let's try to get it simple again. Do you dispute that Mr. Markac had the authority, whether he ever used it is a different matter, but whether -- that he the authority to instruct you to take disciplinary measures against one of your subordinates if he was aware of any undisciplined behaviour? Do you dispute that, or do you agree with Ms. Mahindaratne on this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because of the way in which the Ministry of the Interior functioned in layers and the fact that the assistant minister was on the specialist collegium, it is possible that certain breaches of discipline were discussed at that level, and that it was on the General's insistence that some of the disciplinary proceedings were initiated. So I'm not disputing the fact that perhaps General Markac may have insisted that disciplinary proceedings be initiated in relation to certain breaches of discipline. So I'm not denying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And he did that within the limits of his authority, from what I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvrk, I called this document up prior to the Chamber's questioning. Perhaps if could you look at this. I just wanted to point this out to you, since you that said that General Markac's disciplinary authority was only in relation to the -- the helicopter unit and Lucko Unit. But, however, upon clarification now, I don't need to go through this. But do you agree that although -- I withdraw that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the matter has become clear --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- without the document, then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cvrk, there was a discussion about statistics relating to discipline. Mr. Mikulicic dealt with that, and I believe the document, D528 - we don't need that document on the screen - you were shown statistics provided by -- in relation to your unit as well as other units and there was a discussion between you and the Chamber also. Now, I'd like to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if I could have P2370.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The document you're going to see will be extracts of the MUP employment code.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could go to -- in the English that would be the -- the second document on the e-court. And the Croatian version, page 16. That would be Article -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, as you can see, you'll see in a moment, in the Croatian version, Article 48 lists out what minor infringement is and Article 49 lists out what a major infringement, a serious infringement of work discipline is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in the English, if could you move to the next page, Mr. Registrar, as well as the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There are 26 types of conduct that came within the description of serious infringement of work discipline. Therefore, would you agree with me that those statistics which show specific numbers of disciplinary processes meted out in relation to members of the separate units would not provide the Trial Chamber with any guidance as to exactly what type of conduct was subject to those disciplinary measures? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: I do understand your question. But as you put it yourself, in those disciplinary proceedings involving major breaches of discipline, there are 26 different items envisaged. And it would not have been possible for us to make a description of what the minor or major breach of discipline was. However, it never was a problem to examine each and every one of these breaches of discipline in detail to see what exactly they involved, and if I recall correctly, we even had several instances which involved crimes, and at the end of disciplinary proceedings it so happened that the individuals concerned were fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have P1155.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, for example, you can see in this order, General Markac has requested disciplinary proceedings against a member of the Lucko Unit for his failure to respond to an order to participate in training. Now, you would agree with me, isn't it, therefore, that those numbers, those statistics, include all these type of infringements which were also considered under the MUP employment code as serious breaches of discipline?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: That's right, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you aware, Mr. Cvrk, that Mr. Markac had the authority to directly suspend a member of the -- of any one of the special police units, if he found them to have committed a breach of discipline?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: If this authority was transferred on him by the minister of the interior, then that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question is: Were -- are you aware that that was the case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: As I wasn't working in the special police sector, I am not 100 per cent aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvrk, you were the commander of the special police unit of Zagreb. Now, as the commander, were you not aware that the commander of the special police sector, Mr. Markac, had the authority to suspend a member of your unit, if he considered that necessary, in the interests of discipline of the special police?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I just want to ask for a little clarification. Is that in general or in certain circumstances? It's a pretty broad question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think it is specific enough, Mr. President. I just can't figure out how to narrow it down any further. It's a very straightforward question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the issue is not the matter raised by Mr. Kuzmanovic. However, the problem may be there in view of the previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's why I -- my -- I just wanted to bring him to his particular specific position since he used the word "sector" I believe as a command --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although the problem was higher up, I think. It was -- he said if the authority was transferred upon him by the minister of the interior, then that is correct and he could not -- But --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question would be more factual Mr. President, whether he is aware, not in an argumentative --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne. Please keep in mind what I just said. Putting next questions to overcome an uncertainty without clearly identifying that uncertainty for the next answer is not something that assists the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. Let me call up my document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I have document 609, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that a P Document, I'm assuming?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvrk, do you note Mr. Markac's order to the commander of the anti-terrorist unit Lucko, where he proposes for initiating a disciplinary procedure and the decision on suspension from duty. He reads: "To bring to your attention and for further use, we hereby submit this proposal for initiating a disciplinary procedure against a member of the ATJ Lucko," and the name is recorded, "and the decision on suspension from duty?" And can you read the rest of the document. Do you note my point that General Markac had the authority to suspend a member of a special police unit directly, if he deemed it necessary?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: I wish to clarify the previous question [as interpreted] and try to answer your question; namely, the disciplinary rules of the MUP of the Republic of Croatia says that a decision on suspension can be taken by the minister of the interior or a person authorised accordingly by him. As I worked as part of the police administration of Zagreb, the person that he authorised is the chief of the police administration. As here, we're talking about a member of the anti-terrorist unit of Lucko which is a part of the special police sector there is a possibility that, in relation to these members of the special police sector, including the helicopter unit, including the anti-terrorist unit of Lucko, the minister had authorised in accordance with his own authority General Markac, among others. But I didn't know about this when I received a decision about this from the chief of the special police -- from the police administration. So that is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvrk, in fact, the chief of the police administration of Zadar-Knin police administration testified here, Mr. Cetina. Have you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And in fact his testimony about his authority or what he could do with the special police unit attached to his police administration was completely contrary to what you are saying. And let me read that to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have D1745, please. For the record, that's the statement of the Witness Cetina. And if we could go --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. It's not on the list of cross documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is testimony in court, the statement of a witness is testimony in court. It's not a document. That generally we do not list testimony transcript numbers or statement numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if the document here serves to put to the witness what is the equivalent of oral testimony, that is, attested witness statements --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have a problem with that, Your Honour. Normally we attach witness statements to our exhibit lists if it is marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I also heard you say that you have no problem with it. You wanted to put it on the record and that's it. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne -- no, it depends on what Mr. Kehoe --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have a problem with this. I mean, the practice has been, throughout this, we are listing exhibits that each side is going to use. And this is a piece of evidence that is given an exhibit number, admitted into evidence, and that we've had -- routinely done that. I am somewhat surprised - I'm shocked, I should say - by the comment by counsel that this is not a piece of evidence that needs to be disclosed. Because that clearly has not been the practice since March of 2008.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I may respond Mr. President. This is testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course, you can -- I must admit that I have no clear recollection whether, always, this has been done but on -- let's just assume it -- it was done. It certainly is not done -- specific portions of the testimony of a witness were not identified in advance. Now, here we are a bit at a cross-roads of, on the one hand, a statement which is, as I said before, equivalent to testimony given in court. And, at the same time, being exhibited and not being just transcript references. So, therefore, I have not given it -- and I could discuss it with my colleagues. Now Mr. Kuzmanovic said that he just wanted to have this on the record. Mr. Kehoe, is it a matter, you would say, it cannot be put to the witness or is it something that we could perhaps, in a quiet moment, further discuss what we expect the parties to do? I mean, is your concern at this moment in relation to this question put to this witness, or is it a kind of a general observation that you are concerned about what Ms. Mahindaratne said?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am -- I am not raising a concern with regard to this witness. I'm raising a more global concern that we raised in an e-mail with the OTP recently. And Chambers, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I suggest that we try not to -- for us to observe this battle or for you to fight this battle in the presence of the witness who -- where apparently there is no specific problem in putting this to him. Ms. Mahindaratne, the matter is not off the table but we proceed with this witness at this moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I proceed on this particular issue, Mr. President, or is that an indication that I should not address it at this stage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, can you put to the witness as you intended to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if we could move to page 4 of this -- in the English statement, and in the Croatian version, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you see, Mr. Cvrk, if you could focus on the -- in the English version, the fourth paragraph and can you see -- I'm referring to the paragraph that starts with: "There were also so-called special police units. They were not under the command of the police administration but were directly answerable to the MUP. They had a different building, different uniforms, and they were not doing regular police duties. According to the law, in peacetime, their professional tasks were the prevention of bigger unrest, resolving hijacking, kidnapping and similar jobs." Then a few lines below, he says: "I did not know what their tasks were, if they had any, which they coordinated directly with the MUP headquarters. I personally was not involved in drafting their plans. The special police units had also" -- and then he -- a couple of lines below: "The commander of the special police unit in Zadar was Svemir Vrsaljko. I do not know how many people were under his command. I have never been informed about the special tasks undertaken by those special police units. I never had any meetings with representatives of the special police units. At the time of Storm, I had no control over the special police. The police system that I was in was designed for peacetime, not wartime." And then, Mr. Cvrk, he was further asked about his disciplinary authority over special police units in court, and this is transcript reference page 23593, and this is what was asked and this is his testimony: "Now, isn't it correct that if a member of the special police forces committed an offence, that requests for disciplinary procedure, initiation of disciplinary procedures had to be made by the commander of the special police sector and not yourself? "Yes, that's how it was." This is Mr. Cetina's testimony, which is quite different to what you are saying here. Can you reconcile his testimony with what you are saying here, or do you want to clarify what you have stated so far?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN CVRK
utterances.text: Everything I said so far is based on the rules of the Ministry of Interior. There are disciplinary rules of the Ministry of Interior relating to discipline, and everything else that I was talking about, the interior structure, the way it all operated, how certain orders were submitted through chiefs of police administrations, and engagement of special police units in joint forces, all of that is very transparent. and just as my police administration chief received everything, I cannot see any reason why the chief of the Zadar and Knin police administration, Mr. Cetina, would not receive it. Why Mr. Cetina stated this, I don't know, and I couldn't tell but, at the time when he was appointed the chief of the police administration, he was one of the younger people, as far as I can remember, and de facto upon his appointment he needed to learn much more than others and I think this is visible from his statement. One part of his statement, for me, demonstrates a lack of knowledge of the position to which he was appointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, I'm looking at the clock. We're already three minutes late. Therefore, we will adjourn for the day. Mr. Cvrk, I would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, irrespective of whether that is testimony you've given today or whether that's testimony still to be given tomorrow. Then we would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00, because we adjourn, and we'll resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 1st of December, 9.00, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 1st of December, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.49 p.m.,
